overview: Two types of nervous tissue distinguished by composition and colour, reflecting their different roles in processing versus transmitting signals.
genZNote: Gray matter: where the actual processing happens. White matter: the insulated cables carrying the signal between processing centres.

aspects.label: Main Composition
aspects.valueA: Contains neuron cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated fibres.
aspects.valueB: Contains myelinated nerve fibres (axons) that connect different brain/spinal regions.

aspects.label: Function
aspects.valueA: Site of synaptic processing and integration of information.
aspects.valueB: Transmits electrical signals rapidly between different regions of gray matter.

aspects.label: Reason for Colour
aspects.valueA: Appears grayish due to lack of myelin.
aspects.valueB: Appears white due to the fatty myelin sheath around axons.

aspects.label: Location Pattern
aspects.valueA: Outer layer (cortex) in the brain, but inner (central) in the spinal cord.
aspects.valueB: Inner region in the brain, but outer (peripheral) in the spinal cord.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Gray and white matter swap relative positions between the brain (gray outside, white inside) and the spinal cord (white outside, gray inside, forming a butterfly shape) — a classic diagram-based exam trap.
overlay.memoryTrick: Gray matter = cell bodies, processing. White matter = myelinated wires, fast transmission.
overlay.commonMisconception: White matter isn't 'inactive' tissue — it's essential for fast communication between different processing centres, not just passive wiring.
